DILG Republic of the Philippines DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR AND LOCAL GOVERNMENT DILG-NAPOLCOM center, EDSA cor. Quezon Avenue, West Triangle, Quezon City www.dilq.qov.ph DILG OPINION No. 02 s. 2024 JAN MR. DENJO P. BONILLA danidenjo@gmail.com Dear Mr. Bonilla: This pertains to your electronic mail dated October 9, 2023 requesting the Department's guidance on the possible remedies that can be undertaken in case of the unbearable noise produced by a certain restaurant-bar near your area, operating from 8:00 in the evening until 4:00 in the morning. Per your allegation, despite repeated demands, the said establishment has been doing live-band activities during Fridays, Saturdays and Sundays without soundproof facility to limit their loud music, and without respecting the peace of mind of the neighborhood. For this, you initially sought the assistance of the barangay police. However, they told you that they cannot do anything considering that the said establishment has a business permit. Thus, your request for an opinion on: (I) whether the establishment having business permit is legally allowed to make such noise until the wee hours of the morning; (2) whether there are any liabilities on the part of the Barangay Officials with such inaction; and (3) remedies available to the families affected and what is the process of abatement of nuisance, and whether it can be considered nuisance. As to your first and third queries, we agree with you that noise, when not controlled and goes beyond the safe levels, is hazardous to the eardrums and the brain. Excessive or unusually loud sound may endanger the health the safety of the public. Under RA 7160 or the Local Government Code of 1991, declaration, prevention or abatement of any nuisance, including noise, is devolved to cities and municipalities. Accordingly, these city and municipal officials should ensure the compliance of the establishments within their respective jurisdictions of the technical requirements of tolerable sound levels. Corollary thereto, may we correct the erroneous interpretation that a business establishment, once issued with a business permit is already allowed to make intolerable noise until the wee hours of the morning. In a number of jurisprudence, the Supreme Court comprehensively discussed the nature of a business or Mayor's permit, to wit: "Matlno, Mahusay at Maaasahan" Trunkline No.: 8876-34-54

I) Roble Arrastre vs. Villaflor, et al.l "Section of the Local Government Code of 1991 takes its cue from Section 16 thereof. which is larqelY an exercise of deleqated police power. We said: The general welfare clause is the deleqation in statutory form of the police power of the State to LGUs. Through this. LGUs may prescribe requlations to protect the lives. health. and property of their constituents and maintain peace and order within their respective territorial iurisdictions. Accordingly, we have upheld enactments providing, for instance, the regulation of gambling, the occupation of rig drivers, the installation and operation of pinball machines, the maintenance and operation of cockpits, the exhumation and transfer of corpses from public burial grounds, and the operation of hotels, motels, and lodging houses as valid exercises by local legislatures of the police power under the general welfare clause. Section 444(b)(3)(iv) of the Local Government Code of 1991, whereby the power of the respondent mayor to issue license and permits is circumscribed, is a manifestation of the delegated police power of a municipal corporation." (Emphasis Supplied) 2) Lacap vs. Sandiganbayan2, viz: "As Section 444(b)(3)(iv) so states, the power of the municipal mayor to issue licenses is pursuant to Section 16 of the Local Government Code of 1991, which declares: SEC. 16. General Welfare. - Every local government unit shall exercise the powers expressly granted, those necessarily implied therefrom, as well as powers necessary, appropriate, or incidental for its efficient and effective governance, and those which are essential to the promotion of the general welfare. Within their respective territorial jurisdictions, local government units shall ensure and support, among other things, the preservation and enrichment of culture, promote health and safety, enhance the right of the people to a balanced ecology, encourage and support the development of appropriate and self-reliant scientific and technological capabilities, improve public morals, enhance economic prosperity and social justice, promote full employment among their residents, maintain peace and order, and preserve the comfort and convenience of their inhabitants. Section 16, known as the general welfare clause, encapsulates the delegated police power to local governments. Local qovernment units exercise police power throuqh their respective Ieqislative bodies. Evidently. the Local Government Code of 1991 is unequivocal that the municipal mayor has the power to issue licenses and permits and suspend or revoke the same for any violation of the conditions upon which said licenses or permit> had been issued. pursuant to law or ordinance. x x x (Emphasis Supplied) 3) The City of Bacolod vs. Phuture Visions Co., Inc.3, thus: I G.R. 128509, August 22, 2006. 2 G.R. No. 198162, June 21, 2017, 3 G.R. No. 1920289, January 17, 2018. Page 2 of 4

"xxx while the authority of city mayors to issue or grant licenses and business permits is granted by the Local Government Code (LGC), which also vests local government units with corporate powers, one of which is the power to sue and be sued, this Court has held that the power to issue or grant licenses and business permits is not an exercise of the qovernment's proprietary function. Instead. it is in an exercise of the police power of the State. erqo a qovernmental act. This is clearly elucidated by the Court in Acebedo Optical Company, Inc. v. The Honorable Court of Appeals: The Court of Appeals erred in adjudging subject business permit as having been issued by respondent City Mayor in the performance of proprietary functions of Iligan City. As hereinabove elaborated upon, the issuance of business licenses and permits by a municipality or city is essentially requlat001 in nature. The authority. which devolved upon local qovernment units to issue or qrant such licenses or permits. is essentiallv in the exercise of the police power of the State within the contemplation of the qeneral welfare clause of the Local Government Code. (Emphasis Supplied) From the foregoing, while it may be true that business or Mayor's permit are issued to business establishments, the same is not an absolute authority for the grantee to conduct any activity. If you can take a look of the standard business permit, there are conditions upon which it is issued, which could either be subsumed in a law or in an ordinance. Violation of said conditions warrant revocation thereof by the city or municipal mayor. Such revocation is only in keeping with the principle that the power to grant includes the power to withhold or recall. In your e-mail, you failed to mention the specific local government unit where your residence is located. Be that as it may, you are hereby advised to verify whether your local government unit has an ordinance regulating the operation of bars, beerhouses and other similar establishments or refreshments. Specifically, kindly check on the prescribed days and hours of operation, along with the penalty in case of violation. If it turns out that there was a violation, you are further advised to write the concerned Mayor and discuss the details about the violation of the business establishment and call for the abatement of the noise or if not, revocation of its business permit. On the second querv, if you have reason to believe that the barangay officials fail to perform their duties taking into account the existing ordinance within your local government unit, you can file an administrative case against them pursuant to Sections 604 and 61 of the Local Government Code of 1991 (LGC). 4 Section 60. Grounds for Disciplinary Actions. - An elective local official may be disciplined. suspended, or removed from office on any of the following grounds: (a) Disloyalty to the Republic of the Philippines; (b) Culpable violation of the Constitution; (c) Dishonesty, oppression, misconduct in office, gross negligence, or dereliction of duty; (d) Commission of any offense involving moral turpitude or an offense punishable by at least prision mayor, (e) Abuse of authority; (f) Unauthorized absence for fifteen (15) consecutive working days, except in the case of members of the sangguniang panlalawigan, sangguniang panlungsod, sangguniang bayan, and sangguniang barangay; (g) Application for, or acquisition of, foreign citizenship or residence or the status of an immigrant of another country; and (h) Such other grounds as may be provided in this Code and other laws. This opinion shall be without prejudice to any contrary opinion rendered by more competent authorities and/or the courts. We hope to have guided you accordingly. Thank you.
